title: Plato vs The Algorithm: Beauty is the path to virtue
subtitle: What Plato got right about beauty
author: Panos Paris
introduction: In an age when beauty is shaped by algorithms and commercial pressure, it’s easy to dismiss it as shallow or morally corrosive. Yet, philosopher Panos Paris claims, this is a profound misunderstanding. For most of history, beauty was seen not as a trap, but as a necessary precondition for virtue: a capacity that, properly cultivated, could train our desires toward the good. If beauty shapes our desires from infancy, then rather than resisting its influence, we should harness it, rebuild our aesthetic taste, and even reshape our environments so that beauty becomes a compass for virtue rather than a force that deforms it.
body:
Over the last decade or so, I’ve been thinking about beauty, especially in relation to virtue and related values. Some of the evidence concerning the relationship between beauty and morality is truly eye-opening. People who are found more beautiful are treated better (and, unsurprisingly, those deemed ugly are punished for it): mothers spend more time with prettier babies and children; good-looking people are hired more often and subsequently paid more; they get better treatment by teachers at school; they are better looked after by doctors; they are more leniently judged in court; and are more likely to be assisted by strangers in their time of need. Incidentally, humans aren’t the only victims of our beauty biases. In our environmental concerns, we seem to prioritize habitats and landscapes that are scenic or picturesque; to protect animals that look cuddly and cute; and to oppose the culling of animals that we find attractive, even if that leads to the depletion of ecosystems.

Explanations for such findings often cite phenomena such as the well-known “halo effect”; this is when some of our global judgments (including beauty judgments) unconsciously affect our more specific judgments (including being fair, smart, likeable, or, as it turns out, green). Such unconscious influences, like all unconscious influences, can creep into our behavior, decisions, and even dreams, desires, and aspirations, unawares. It’s thus no wonder that beauty exercises a profound influence over our lives, far greater than many of us would like to admit. But what does such influence tell us about the relationship between beauty and virtue? Many would haste to point out that beauty and virtue pull in very different directions. If so, then anyone seeking to cultivate virtue had better tie themselves to the proverbial mast so as to guard against the siren-like power of beauty.

Beauty exercises a profound influence over our lives, far greater than many of us would like to admit.

This position, which starkly contrasts beauty and virtue, may seem all the more attractive today, when the word “beauty” brings to mind “Instagram faces,” so-called beauty salons, and a bunch of celebrities or so-called beauty influencers. When I discuss beauty with my students, they instinctively say that “beauty is in the eye of the beholder” and that beauty is a matter of individual preferences––to each their own.

Ironically, most of these students pursue a very recognizable kind of look, and partake of the various institutions (e.g., the beauty industry) and platforms (e.g., social media, photo-editing apps, etc.) that promulgate it. Pointing this out hardly helps to convince them that such beauty trends, far from being sincere expressions of their autonomy and individuality, seem to operate more like an aesthetic, cognitive, and affective straitjacket.

To illustrate this, I probe the question of beauty from a different angle, asking my students how they experience beauty: when you see someone beautiful, I ask, how do you feel? The answers I get range from blank stares to “nothing,” “jealous,” or “bad about myself.” Apparently, platforms like Instagram, which currently hold the monopoly on beauty, not only generate a narrow profile of what counts as beautiful, but also numb young people to the potentialities of beauty, turning its power against themselves, to the point where personal appearance has become the source of a major public health concern.

This conception of beauty––call it i-Beauty––seems, of course, worlds apart from what someone like Keats must have had in mind when he wrote that “a thing of beauty is a joy forever”, or that “Beauty is truth, truth beauty,––that is all. Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know”.

Likewise, it seems impossible to square the modern identification of beauty with “Instagrammability,” with views of philosophers like Plato, who identified beauty with goodness or virtue. What do Instagrammable looks have to do with goodness or virtue? If i-Beauty is all the beauty there is, then perhaps the answer is: nothing. But while our culture is hellbent on inscribing this conception as the be all and end all of beauty, such i-Beauty is only the tip of an iceberg, the depth of which is far greater than contemporary orthodoxy would have us think––and, by the way, such orthodoxy includes not just popular culture but much of the mainstream of academic philosophical discourse as well.

Philosophers like Hume or Smith gave pride of place to a kind of beauty that is largely forgotten today: that of the virtues themselves and of the virtuous, that is, those who possess the virtues.

By contrast, philosophers prior to the nineteenth century, and going all the way back to antiquity, had a very different take on beauty. One of the main differences between the modern aesthetic sensibility and that of someone like Aristotle or Confucius (and even Hume or Schopenhauer) is that they were open to a far wider palette of beauties than seem like live options today. Few contemporary philosophers have the openness to beauty to say, with Roger Scruton, that “there are beautiful propositions as well as beautiful worlds, beautiful proofs as well as beautiful snails, even beautiful diseases and beautiful deaths.”

Far from the narrow conception of i-Beauty, which has evolved through our virtual and visual media, beauty can be found in the most surprising places, so long as we have the wisdom, courage, and openness to find it. It should therefore come as no surprise that philosophers like Hume or Smith gave pride of place to a kind of beauty that is largely forgotten today: that of the virtues themselves and of the virtuous, that is, those who possess the virtues. This kind of beauty, which they called “moral beauty,” suggests a far more intimate connection between beauty and virtue than might be expected given today’s near equation between beauty in general and i-Beauty,

This shouldn’t surprise us: after all, generally speaking, beauty undoubtedly is, or at least should be, the source of great pleasure. When we find something beautiful, it comes into focus and delights us in a way that few other things do. The only comparison could be something like looking into the eyes of your favorite grandparent or lying in the arms of your beloved. This pleasure sets off a chain of desire, consciously or unconsciously, to pursue, emulate, serve the object, and make it part of one’s life. Such a desire can have a profound impact on us. We cherish and nourish the beautiful, and this is precisely why we find that beautiful people are disproportionately treated better than their less fortunate counterparts. Notwithstanding its undesirable consequences, such a response seems overwhelmingly positive and is a basic ingredient for happiness. None of this should surprise anyone who has had genuine experiences of beauty.

But beauty isn’t just a source of pleasure; it’s also special in that it is, somehow, its own reward. Why, other than that they’re beautiful, do people look at flowers, sunsets, or the paintings of Botticelli? It seems to me that, so long as they are, in fact, responsive to the beauty of such objects, as opposed to, say, their fame, monetary value, and the like, experiencing them becomes for them its own reward. But isn’t this precisely what we should expect of goodness as well? The virtuous, that is, aren’t courageous, kind, honest, or fair because they expect a payoff––they hold these values and live according to them for their own sake. This should become obvious once we consider who we would find more virtuous: someone who loves goodness and delights in being kind and courageous, or someone who thinks they have to act kindly and courageously, and constantly suppresses their desires to do so? If, like me, you find the first type of person more attractive, the reason has to do with beauty. Sure, the first type of person may be called more beautiful because of their greater inner harmony. But that’s not all. What’s more important is that the truly virtuous person finds virtue beautiful and this is, at least in part, wherein their virtue lies.

SUGGESTED READING The pursuit of beauty is fragmenting the self By Ellen Atlanta

Perhaps, then, the question is not: does whatever we find beautiful lead us to virtue? Instead, it is: can the capacity to feel beauty––which is revealed both in some experiences of i-Beauty but also in experiences of moral beauty and other kinds of beauty––help us cultivate virtue? If there is such a thing as moral beauty, then an affirmative answer to this question seems highly plausible. But, of course, this presupposes that the notion of moral beauty is a conceptually coherent one, something that many today might find difficult to accept.

One concern may be that talk of virtue as “beautiful” mistakes a metaphor for literalness. Even if there’s more to beauty than i-Beauty, is it not nonetheless still true that beauty is about looks, that is, appearances? And can’t appearances mislead or conceal the reality of something? Yes and no. It seems right to say that beauty trades in appearances, but appearances shouldn’t be narrowly construed in terms of visual appearances; after all, music can be beautiful too. Nor should we limit the realm of the beautiful to the realm of the perceptible: abstract objects can also be beautiful, as mathematicians’ talk of the beauty of proofs or physicists’ talk of beautiful theories should teach us.

Now, when it comes to objects that can be seen, felt, heard, or otherwise perceived through one or more of our five senses, appearances can mislead. For instance, a piece of music can sound simple but be extraordinarily complex. Or, more to the point, a person can be physically beautiful but be a horrible person. If we take that person’s physical appearance as a clue to their personality, then appearances will, indeed, mislead. But far from being proof that beauty and virtue are at odds, this kind of experience may be one of the most familiar confirmations of the view that virtue is, in fact, a kind of beauty, just as vice is a kind of ugliness––and here, at the realm of personality, which is abstract, appearances, once grasped properly (for we can, of course, also be mistaken about someone’s personality), no longer mislead.

Consider this: haven’t you ever come across someone who initially looks physically beautiful, only to find them ugly once you got to know them better? Or, conversely, maybe you’ve found someone physically unattractive, only to later come to find them beautiful upon getting to know them? I know I have, and evidence suggests I’m not alone. Similarly, few of us would be comfortable thinking of our beloved grandparents as ugly, though they are past the peak of their physical attractiveness. All of this suggests that physical beauty isn’t the only species of beauty available to our experience, even if we live in a culture that not just fails to highlight this fact but actively seeks to hide it.

If that’s true, and as long as we recognize virtue among the colors in our palette of beauties, as it were, then it looks like there should be a pathway to virtue through beauty. People are born finding certain people, colors, animals, and other objects, beautiful (which they seem to be: babies only a few weeks old tend to look for longer at people with faces that adults would rate as beautiful). These initial experiences of beauty can serve as foundations upon which we can anchor the rest of their aesthetic sensibilities through chains of association. Isn’t this what we do with all sorts of other things that we come to enjoy by acquiring a taste for them, whether that’s eating healthy, exercising, or engaging in challenging but rewarding activities?

On this view, beauty is not just a feature that objects have, like symmetry or balance. It is, more importantly, the object of an experience which we, as human beings (and perhaps other animals too), have the capacity to undergo. It combines different aspects of what makes us human: it combines our mammalian reward signal––pleasure––with our capacity for reflection and self-reflection that enable us to work certain things out and question our judgments, including our judgments about value. We are uniquely capable of educating, shaping, and reshaping our ideas, feelings, and responses. And all of this is also true of beauty and of where we find it. But just like our food and drink or lifestyle preferences, that’s both a curse and a blessing, for it means that we can develop a taste for things that are bad for us, just as easily as we can harmonize what is good for us with what we find beautiful.

Assuming we want to follow the latter, that is, the healthy, virtuous path––how might we go about doing so? Perhaps surprisingly, I think that Plato’s Symposium gives us some clues about how we can practically harness beauty to instill virtue. There, Plato has Diotima, a priestess whose views on beauty seem to be those espoused in the text, describe what’s known as the Ladder of Love. On this account, people begin by finding beautiful and loving beautiful bodies; but this offers educators the opportunity to draw people’s attention to the similarities between such beautiful bodies and beautiful souls; then they can go on to relate the beauty of those souls to the beauty of the law, the beauty of wisdom, and so on.

The diet of associations upon which we graze is of paramount importance, thereby placing the Herculean task on anyone who cares to promote virtue to steer learners in the right direction.

I think that there are at least three lessons we can draw from this. First, we need to remind ourselves that hierarchies matter when it comes to value––the ladder ascends, it isn’t horizontal. If we don’t believe that being virtuous is more important than being wealthy or popular, for instance, then an essential ingredient for forging a pathway from beauty to virtue is just not there.

Second, at least sometimes, language matters: “beauty” and “beautiful” are among the words we hear on a very regular basis. They are also among the words a child will hear very early on and will undoubtedly learn to associate with pleasurable experiences and with all sorts of positive qualities (not least via pleasure). It is therefore crucial that parents, teachers, and anyone with an interest in promoting virtue ensure that the idea that virtue is beautiful is marked clearly on their intellectual and affective cartography. At least one way to do this is to ensure that we speak appropriately and use “beauty” and “beautiful” not just when referring to people who are physically attractive (who, incidentally, are not just people whose looks are “Instagrammable”), but also to people who are kind, caring, courageous, fair, and so on.

Finally, our taste, by which I mean our disposition to find certain things beautiful and others ugly, is largely founded upon chains of associative experiences. Nobody knows this better than those responsible for our media, advertising and, of course, the beauty industry itself. All it takes for someone to go and consume something that is both costly and likely also bad for them is to conjure in their mind an association between that thing and something that they are sure to like: a physically attractive body, a symbol of wealth, a promise of happiness (which, by the way, for Stendhal, is precisely what beauty amounts to). What does this mean for the development of our taste? It means that the diet of associations upon which we graze is of paramount importance, thereby placing the Herculean task on anyone who cares to promote virtue to steer learners in the right direction

It’s worth bearing in mind, though, that the reason this task is so momentous is not that the beauty of virtue is so hard to develop a taste for: people can be educated to do extraordinarily complex things. But the game is rigged: we are all constantly bombarded by media that have no stake at all in us developing virtue––indeed, our virtue is their loss. This means that we need legislation and regulation both in terms of content and access. It should not be okay to present as beautiful bodies and faces that are unhealthy or doctored; and it should be possible to navigate public spaces without being bombarded by such images in the first place. Moreover, for whatever dominant mode of beauty is being promoted, there needs to be a culture of education and promotion of alternatives that are, on the one hand, highlighting the beauty of virtue, and, on the other, encouraging a critical stance towards mainstream culture. Ultimately, we need to live in a society that includes institutions that resist profit-driven interests and promote varieties of beauty that are healthy––for our bodies, our minds, and our characters.

We are thus faced with a choice, assuming we care about virtue: we can choose to reprimand those who care about beauty, treat them as superficial, and seek to always be vigilant against beauty’s influence on our judgment. Or we can harness the power of beauty, harmonize it with our conceptions of the good, and use education to instill a rich and diverse sensibility that finds beauty in far more than can be dreamt through the blinkers of visual, virtual culture. There’s a catch, though. For unless both individuals and society face up to both the power and importance of beauty, and introduce infrastructure and legislation that facilitate aesthetic education, then this will remain a dream for all but the most quixotic among us.
